nodes.label: Differential Equations
nodes.note: A differential equation links a function to its derivatives. JEE Main tests classification, standard solvable types, and forming equations from arbitrary constants.

nodes.label: Order and Degree
nodes.note: First classify the equation: how high a derivative appears, and what power it carries. Many JEE one-markers stop right here.

nodes.label: Order of a DE
nodes.note: The order is the highest derivative present. $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + 3\frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0$ has order 2; $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^3 = x$ has order 1.

nodes.label: Degree of a DE
nodes.note: The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is cleared of radicals and fractions. The degree is the power of the highest-order derivative after the equation is cleared of radicals and fractions. Rationalise first, then read off the power of the top derivative.

nodes.label: Example: Degree Check
nodes.note: $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 + \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0$ has order 2 and degree 1, since the highest derivative appears to the first power.

nodes.label: General and Particular Solutions
nodes.note: Solving a DE means recovering the family of functions and then, if an initial condition is given, one member of it.

nodes.label: General Solution
nodes.note: A general solution of an $n$-th order DE contains $n$ independent arbitrary constants: $y = c_1 e^x + c_2 e^{-x}$ for a second-order equation. The number of constants matches the order.

nodes.label: Particular Solution
nodes.note: A particular solution fixes the constants using an initial condition, e.g. $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 0$. This turns the family curve into the single curve through the given point with given slope.

nodes.label: Example: Fixing Constants
nodes.note: $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x$ gives $y = x^2 + C$; with $y(1) = 3$, $C = 2$, so the particular solution is $y = x^2 + 2$.

nodes.label: Separable Equations
nodes.note: The easiest type: everything about $y$ on one side, everything about $x$ on the other, then integrate both sides.

nodes.label: Separating Variables
nodes.note: $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y)$ becomes $\frac{dy}{g(y)} = f(x)\,dx$, then integrate: $\int \frac{dy}{g(y)} = \int f(x)\,dx + C$. Keep the constant on one side only.

nodes.label: Example: $ rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{y}{x}$
nodes.note: $\frac{dy}{y} = \frac{dx}{x} \Rightarrow \ln|y| = \ln|x| + c \Rightarrow y = Cx$.

nodes.label: Homogeneous Equations
nodes.note: A first-order DE is homogeneous when $\frac{dy}{dx} = F(y/x)$. The substitution $v = y/x$ converts it into a separable one.

nodes.label: The v = y/x Substitution
nodes.note: Put $y = vx$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = v + x\frac{dv}{dx}$. Substituting gives $x\frac{dv}{dx} = F(v) - v$, which is separable in $v$ and $x$.

nodes.label: Example: $ rac{dy}{dx} =  rac{x + y}{x}$
nodes.note: $v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1 + v \Rightarrow x\frac{dv}{dx} = 1 \Rightarrow v = \ln|x| + C \Rightarrow y = x(\ln|x| + C)$.

nodes.label: Linear First-Order Equations
nodes.note: The form $\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)$ is conquered by an integrating factor. This is the most frequently examined type in JEE Main.

nodes.label: Integrating Factor Method
nodes.note: The integrating factor is $I.F. = e^{\int P\,dx}$. Multiplying through makes the left side a perfect derivative: $\frac{d}{dx}(y \cdot I.F.) = Q \cdot I.F.$, so $y \cdot I.F. = \int Q \cdot I.F.\,dx + C$.

nodes.label: Example: $ rac{dy}{dx} +  rac{y}{x} = x$
nodes.note: $I.F. = e^{\int \frac{dx}{x}} = x$, so $\frac{d}{dx}(xy) = x^2 \Rightarrow xy = \frac{x^3}{3} + C \Rightarrow y = \frac{x^2}{3} + \frac{C}{x}$.

nodes.label: Bernoulli Equations
nodes.note: Bernoulli's equation $\frac{dy}{dx} + P y = Q y^n$ looks nonlinear but a substitution linearises it. Spot the power $n$ first.

nodes.label: Reducing to Linear Form
nodes.note: Divide by $y^n$ and set $v = y^{1-n}$, so $\frac{dv}{dx} = (1-n)y^{-n}\frac{dy}{dx}$. The equation in $v$ becomes linear: $\frac{dv}{dx} + (1-n)Pv = (1-n)Q$, then solve by integrating factor.

nodes.label: Orthogonal Trajectories
nodes.note: Two curve families are orthogonal when their tangents meet at right angles, so their slopes are negative reciprocals.

nodes.label: Finding Orthogonal Trajectories
nodes.note: From the given family's DE $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)$, replace it by $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{f(x, y)}$ and solve the new DE. The solution family is the orthogonal trajectory.

nodes.label: Example: Circles Centred at Origin
nodes.note: $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$ gives $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$; the orthogonal slope is $\frac{y}{x}$, whose solution $y = Cx$ is the family of lines through the origin.

nodes.label: Formation from Arbitrary Constants
nodes.note: The reverse problem: given a family with $n$ arbitrary constants, eliminate them to build the DE. Differentiate $n$ times and purge the constants.

nodes.label: Eliminating Constants
nodes.note: Differentiate the relation as many times as there are constants, then use the resulting equations to delete every $c_i$. The leftover relation among $x, y$ and derivatives is the required DE, of order $n$.

nodes.label: Example: $y = Ae^x + B$
nodes.note: $y' = Ae^x$, $y'' = Ae^x$, so $y'' = y'$, i.e. $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} - \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$. Two constants give a second-order DE.
